Rosa Parks. The African-American civil rights activist whose refusal to surrender her bus seat to a white passenger in Montgomery, Alabama on December 1, 1955 sparked the Montgomery Bus Boycott and became a pivotal moment in the Civil Rights Movement. Known as the Mother of the Civil Rights Movement, her act of quiet defiance initiated the cascade of events that established Martin Luther King Jr. as a national leader. She was arrested that day for violating the city's segregation ordinances, despite being seated in the colored section of the bus. Her trial was the catalyst for the Montgomery Bus Boycott, which lasted three hundred eighty-one days and paralyzed the city's transit system. But she was not an accidental activist. She was a seasoned NAACP member with prior activism, and her act was partly planned as a test case against segregation. She suffered harassment and death threats after her arrest and eventually moved to Detroit seeking safety and new opportunities. In 1992 she authored her autobiography Rosa Parks: My Story, which brought her reflections on courage and principle to wider audiences. She became an elder stateswoman of the movement and was celebrated internationally. In 1996 she received the Presidential Medal of Freedom. Her rise enabled King's rise to prominence, as the boycott her arrest triggered became the launchpad for his national career. She was a fellow NAACP organizer with Ella Baker, who became a mentor to the next generation. And younger activists like John Lewis drew inspiration from her example of dignity and resistance, making her legacy a foundation for all who came after.
